notes.heading: Solve constraints using quantities demanded and supplied
paragraphs: An equilibrium satisfies equality between quantity demanded and quantity supplied under the stated curves. A legal price constraint need not clear the market. At a binding ceiling below equilibrium, demand can exceed supply; the difference is a modelled shortage. At a floor above equilibrium, supply can exceed demand. These comparisons do not identify the actual quantity traded unless a rationing or purchase rule is supplied. If a tax creates different buyer and seller prices, include the price wedge explicitly instead of placing the same price into both curves.

questions.prompt: In a fictional market Qd=80-2P and Qs=20+P. Find equilibrium, then the shortage at a binding ceiling P=15.
questions.answer: Equilibrium P=20 and Q=40. At P=15, demand is 50 and supply is 35, so shortage is 15.
solution: Evaluate both quantities at the ceiling and subtract supply from demand.

questions.prompt: A fictional market has Qd=60-Pb and Qs=Ps, where Pb is the buyer price and Ps the seller receipt. A unit tax of 10 imposes Pb=Ps+10. Find both prices and the quantity.
solution: Substitute the price wedge into demand: Qd=50-Ps.
Equate with Qs=Ps, then recover the buyer price.
markingPoints: Find seller receipt 25 and buyer price 35.

questions.prompt: Two observations from a fictional market show both price and quantity increasing. A student concludes demand alone increased. Explain why this is one possible explanation but not a unique identification.
questions.answer: A demand increase with unchanged supply can produce the observations, but simultaneous demand and supply shifts can also do so.
solution: Distinguish observed equilibrium outcomes from the unobserved curves.
For example, demand and supply can both increase, with the demand shift large enough for price to rise.
markingPoints: Identify the demand-only explanation as possible.
Explain that two outcomes do not identify which curves changed.
